notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 39:1–22, drawing on the available sources from the searched sites.

---

## Exodus 39:1–22 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Garments of Ministry
**Traditional reading:** The “cloths of service” (KJV) or “specially woven garments” were distinct from the “holy garments for Aaron.” The phrase was previously used in Ex 31:10 for the wrappings that covered the sacred furniture during the march. Here it is applied to priestly vestments, meaning they were not for display or daily wear but exclusively for sanctuary service. Bush (cited at Precept Austin) ties this to Rev 7:13–15, where those in white robes “serve him day and night in his temple.” Henry notes: “Those upon whom honour is put, from them service is expected.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

Gill notes that some Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) understood “cloths of service” to refer not to priestly garments at all but to the coverings used to wrap the sanctuary vessels during travel (Num 4:5). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/39.htm

The refrain “just as the LORD had commanded Moses” appears seven times in Exodus 39, which Precept Austin’s Thompson says is especially emphatic for the priestly garments because the high priest was “the most prominent type of Christ” in the whole tabernacle system (citing George Bush). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

**Reformed / Ligonier:** The garments of Aaron were made of the same colors and design as the tabernacle itself (Ex 26; 28:1–39). When the high priest was seen, he looked like a “mini-tabernacle”—an anticipation of the incarnate temple to come (John 2:13–22). — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/special-garments-aaron

---

### v. 2 — Bezalel Made the Ephod
**Traditional reading:** The singular “he” indicates Bezalel as the chief craftsman. The ephod was a sleeveless vest worn close to the body, probably extending just below the hips, made of the same materials as the inner tabernacle curtains: gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary (Thompson); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-39/

The Catholic Encyclopedia describes the ephod as having three parts: a kind of waistcoat or bodice (the main oblong piece, bound under the arms to the waist), two shoulder-pieces, and a girdle. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05497a.htm

---

### v. 3 — Gold Threads Woven In
**Traditional reading:** This is the only biblical description of how gold thread was produced: gold was beaten into thin plates, then cut into wires, and twisted together with the colored yarn and linen. Gill cites Maimonides (Cele Hamikdash c. 9 §5) explaining that a single thread of pure gold was twisted with six threads of blue (and so on for each color), yielding four gold threads among twenty-eight total threads. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/39.htm

Ellicott calls this “a very primitive method of forming gold thread… nowhere else mentioned” and notes it “implies a ruder state of the art of metallurgy than we should have expected,” though he adds that a similar embroidery practice existed in Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/39.htm

Thompson (Precept Austin) notes that metalworkers can hammer gold to as thin as “a thousandth of an inch,” making it both durable and flexible for weaving. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

---

### v. 4 — Shoulder Pieces
**Traditional reading:** The shoulder pieces (straps) joined the ephod at its two upper corners so it could be fastened. The Pulpit Commentary simply notes this follows the instructions of Ex 28:7. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/39.htm

---

### v. 5 — The Skillfully Woven Waistband
**Traditional reading:** The waistband (curious girdle, KJV) was woven as one piece *with* the ephod, not a separate attachment—emphasising indivisible unity. The BibleHub topical article notes three theological implications: (1) an indivisible priestly calling—no part of ministry could be separated from the whole; (2) unity of the twelve tribes whose names appear on the onyx stones; (3) integrity of mediation—priest and sacrifice belong together, later fulfilled in Christ who is both Priest and Offering (Heb 9:11–14). Rabbinic tradition (b. Zevahim 88b) linked the girdle to expiation of “impure thoughts.” — https://biblehub.com/q/Ephod_s_design_s_role_in_worship.htm

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The ephod was “held in place with a girdle or sash of the same colors and fabric,” noting the pattern given by the Lord was followed precisely. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-39.html

---

### vv. 6–7 — The Onyx Stones on the Shoulders
**Traditional reading:** The two onyx stones were engraved like signet seals with the names of the twelve sons of Israel (six per stone) and mounted in gold filigree settings on the shoulder pieces. They served as “memorial stones.” The high priest literally bore Israel on his shoulders as he ministered. Precept Austin’s Thompson notes that engraving on stones of this small size “would not be easy,” emphasising the skill involved. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

**Reformed / Ligonier:** Aaron represented the entire nation—not only his fellow tribesmen but all Israel. This was seen in his wearing the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders *and* on his heart (the breastplate). The high priest’s ministry was primarily atonement, covering sins and pointing toward the restoration of Eden’s glory. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/special-garments-aaron

---

### v. 8 — The Breastpiece (Workmanship Like the Ephod)
**Traditional reading:** The breastpiece (ḥoshen) was made of identical materials to the ephod—gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. It was called “the breastplate of judgment” (Ex 28:15) because it held the Urim and Thummim. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary says the breastplate pictures the high priest’s ministry on behalf of Israel and signifies the care which Jesus, the believer’s High Priest, has for His own (Heb 4:14–16). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-39.html

---

### v. 9 — Square, Folded Double, a Span
**Traditional reading:** The breastpiece was square when folded double—a span (about 9 inches / 23 cm) in both length and width. Folding it double created a pouch for the Urim and Thummim. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-39/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/39.htm

---

### vv. 10–14 — The Twelve Gemstones
**Traditional reading:** Four rows of three gemstones each, each stone engraved with a tribe’s name. Precept Austin’s Thompson gives color notes: ruby (deep red), topaz (golden yellow), emerald (green); turquoise (blue-green), sapphire (blue), diamond (clear/smoky); jacinth (orange-red), agate (brown/white), amethyst (deep purple); beryl (greenish-blue), onyx (various/black), jasper (brown/red). He adds: “Aaron is not wearing a robe containing the names of the Muslims or Mormons; but of the twelve sons of Israel.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

The precise identification of the stones is uncertain. The Pulpit Commentary defers to its notes on Ex 28:17–20. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/39.htm

Gill notes an interesting observation: in the account of making the breastplate, the Urim and Thummim are not mentioned, which “seems to confirm the opinion of many, and which is my own, that they are the same with the stones.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/39.htm

---

### vv. 15–18 — Gold Chains and Upper Fastenings
**Traditional reading:** Braided chains of pure gold were made, fastened to the two upper gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece, with the other ends attached to the two gold filigree settings on the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. This suspended the breastpiece from above. Keil & Delitzsch note this follows Ex 28:22–25 precisely. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/exodus/39.htm

---

### vv. 19–21 — Lower Rings, Blue Cord, and Security
**Traditional reading:** Two additional gold rings were placed on the inside lower corners of the breastpiece (next to the ephod), and two corresponding rings on the front of the ephod shoulder pieces, just above the waistband. A blue cord tied the lower rings together so the breastpiece sat above the waistband and would not swing loose. The blue cord is noted by Pett as a detail of careful design—the breastpiece “might not be loosed from the ephod.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/exodus-39.html

The refrain “as the LORD had commanded Moses” closes the breastpiece section (v. 21). Precept Austin notes this exact-obedience refrain is repeated for each major item. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

**Reformed / Ligonier:** The high priest carried the names of Israel on his shoulders (the onyx stones, vv. 6–7) and over his heart (the breastplate stones). He was an intermediary between the holy Creator and sinful people. The stones of the breastplate were found also in Eden (Ezek 28:13), pointing to the restorative hope of atonement. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/special-garments-aaron

---

### v. 22 — The Robe of the Ephod, All of Blue
**Traditional reading:** The robe (me‘îl) worn under the ephod was “all of blue,” the work of a weaver—a seamless, sleeveless tunic put on over the head. Thompson (Precept Austin) describes it as covering the priest from shoulder to foot with an opening at the top, like “a coat of mail” (see v. 23). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds that the color scheme of blue, purple, scarlet, and gold continues in the robe’s design, and that the bells (described in vv. 25–26) let the people outside know the high priest was alive as he ministered within. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-39.html

The Catholic Encyclopedia stresses that the “robe of the ephod” must not be confused with the ephod proper: “The tunick was worn under the ephod; it was a sleeveless frock, made ‘all of violet.’” — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05497a.htm

---

## Denominational Distinctives (Where They Differ)

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The Ligonier devotional stresses typology: the high priest’s garments mirror the tabernacle’s own materials so that Aaron looked like “a mini-tabernacle,” foreshadowing Christ as the incarnate temple (John 2:13–22). Aaron represented both God to Israel and Israel to God—the one mediator. The stones of the breastplate echo the gems of Eden (Ezek 28:13), signalling that the priestly ministry aims at restoring paradise. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/special-garments-aaron

### Baptist
Gill (18th-century Particular Baptist) brings rabbinic sources extensively (Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Maimonides) and suggests the Urim and Thummim were the gemstones themselves. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary sees straightforward typology: the breastplate over the heart pictures Christ’s care for believers (Heb 4:14–16), and it doubled as a pouch for the Urim and Thummim used in judicial decisions. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/39.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-39.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik emphasises practical application: precise obedience in “small details” honours God and brings blessing. The focus is less on scholarly minutiae and more on the faithfulness of the craftsmen and the symbolic weight of bearing Israel’s names before God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-39/

### Catholic
The Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) draws on Josephus and Egyptian monuments to distinguish three parts of the ephod. It emphasises that the ephod was not the high priest’s everyday garb but reserved for ministry and for consulting the Lord via the Urim and Thummim. The Haydock Catholic Commentary notes a distinction in the Hebrew between “clothes of service” (for wrapping tabernacle items) and “the holy garments of Aaron.” The Douay-Rheims (Challoner) renders v. 3 as “with embroidered work” and notes the gold was “drawn small into threads” to be twisted with the coloured wool. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05497a.htm ; https://ccel.org/ccel/challoner/douayrheims/Exodus/39.html

### Lutheran / Conservative (Keil & Delitzsch)
Keil & Delitzsch give a careful structural analysis, noting that the order of garments in Ex 39 is arranged analogously to the sacred furniture in Ex 25–30—with the ephod and the golden frontlet as the two “poles” around which everything else is arranged (citing Baumgarten). They also note that the Urim and Thummim are not mentioned in this chapter, and that the singular “girdle” in v. 29 is a generic singular used collectively for the girdles of all priests. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/exodus/39.htm

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott is historically critical: he notes the “dislocation” of order compared to Ex 28, calls the gold-thread technique “ruder… than we should have expected,” and points out that the gold was embroidered *into* the already-woven fabric (a practice known in Egypt). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/39.htm

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible Notes, via Precept Austin)
The NET note on v. 32 (cited at Precept Austin) observes that the completion of the tabernacle is “the fulfillment of God’s plan revealed at the beginning of the book, i.e., to reside with his people.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary
